problems.title: Find Subtree Sizes After Changes
problems.problem: You get a tree rooted at node 0 as a parent array, and a letter s[i] on every node. For every node x (all at the same time, using the original tree), find the closest ancestor y with the same letter. If it exists, x gets cut from its parent and attached under y. Return the size of every node's subtree in the final tree.

examples.explanation: Node 3 has letter 'a'. Its ancestors are 1 ('b') and 0 ('a'), so node 3 moves under node 0. Nothing else changes. Node 0 now has 6 nodes under it, node 1 keeps 4 and 5, so its size is 3.
Node 2 ('b') moves under node 1 ('b'), and node 4 ('a') moves under node 0 ('a'). The changes happen at the same time. Node 1 ends with child 2, so size 2; node 0 has everything, so size 5.

problems.intuition: While doing a DFS from the root, the current root-to-node path is exactly the list of ancestors. If for each letter we remember the deepest node on the path with that letter (last[c]), then the new parent of x is just last[s[x]] at the moment we enter x. When we leave a node we restore last[c] to what it was before (prev[x]), like a stack per letter. Because a new parent is always an original ancestor, every node still comes after its new parent in the original DFS order, so we can add sizes bottom-up by walking that order backwards.
approach: Build children lists adj from parent. Copy parent into np (new parent).
Set last[26] to -1. Enter the root: last[s[0]] = 0, order[0] = 0.
Run an iterative DFS with stack st and a per-node child pointer idx (no recursion, so a 1e5 deep chain is safe).
When entering child y with letter c: if last[c] != -1 then np[y] = last[c]; save prev[y] = last[c]; set last[c] = y; record y in order.
When a node x has no more children, restore last[s[x]] = prev[x] and pop it.
Set ans[i] = 1 for all, then for i from n-1 down to 1 do ans[np[order[i]]] += ans[order[i]].
Return ans.
dryRun: x=0: y=1 ('b'), last[b] = -1 so np[1] stays 0. prev[1] = -1, last[b] = 1, push 1
x=1: y=3 ('a'), last[a] = 0 so np[3] = 0. prev[3] = 0, last[a] = 3, push 3
x=3: no children, last[a] = prev[3] = 0, pop
x=1: y=4 ('b'), last[b] = 1 so np[4] = 1 (same as before). After 4 finishes, last[b] = 1 again
x=1: y=5 ('c'), last[c] = -1 so np[5] stays 1. Then 1 finishes, last[b] = -1
x=0: y=2 ('a'), last[a] = 0 so np[2] = 0. Then 2 and 0 finish

complexity.time: O(n) since each node is entered and left once
complexity.space: O(n) for adj, stack, order and np

edgeCases: Single node tree: answer is [1]
Chain where every letter is the same: closest same-letter ancestor is the parent itself, so nothing changes
Deep chain of 1e5 nodes: iterative DFS avoids StackOverflowError
Changes use the original tree, not the partly changed one, which is why we read ancestors from the original DFS path
problems.takeaway: Need the nearest ancestor with some property? Keep a per-key 'last seen on the path' during DFS and restore it when you leave the node.

problems.title: Majority Element
problems.problem: Return the element that appears more than n/2 times in the array. Such an element is guaranteed to exist.
problems.intuition: Boyer-Moore voting: pair up each majority element with a different element and cancel both. Since the majority has more than half the elements, it cannot be fully cancelled, so it is the candidate left standing at the end.
approach: Keep cand and cnt, starting at cnt = 0.
For each x: if cnt is 0, take x as the new cand.
If x == cand do cnt++, else cnt--.
Return cand.
dryRun: x=3: cnt is 0 so cand = 3, then cnt = 1
x=3: cnt is 0 so cand = 3, then cnt = 1
edgeCases: Single element: it is the answer
All elements equal
Negative and extreme values like -1e9 work because we only compare
Majority not at the start, like [1,2,1,3,1]
problems.takeaway: More than half means it survives pairwise cancelling: Boyer-Moore voting gives O(1) space. A HashMap count is the easy fallback.

problems.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.problem: A sorted array of unique numbers was rotated some number of times (1 to n). Find the smallest element in O(log n) time.

examples.explanation: The original array was [1,2,3,4,5] rotated 3 times.
The original array was [0,1,2,4,5,6,7] rotated 4 times.
The original array was [11,13,15,17] rotated 4 times, so it looks unrotated.

problems.intuition: Compare the middle with the right end. If nums[mid] > nums[r], the drop (the minimum) must be to the right of mid. Otherwise the part from mid to r is sorted, so the minimum is at mid or to its left. Each step halves the range.
approach: While l < r: mid = l + (r - l) / 2.
If nums[mid] > nums[r], set l = mid + 1 (minimum is strictly right of mid).
Else set r = mid (mid could be the minimum).
Return nums[l].
dryRun: mid = 3: nums[3] = 1 > nums[4] = 2? No, so r = 3
edgeCases: Single element: loop never runs, return it
Not rotated (rotated n times): r keeps moving left to index 0
Two elements like [2,1]
Compare with nums[r], not nums[l], so the unrotated case works without special handling
problems.takeaway: Rotated sorted array: compare mid with the right end to decide which half has the break point.

problems.title: Permutations
problems.problem: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible orderings (permutations). Any order of the result is fine.
problems.intuition: Build the permutation one slot at a time. For the next slot, try every number not used yet (vis), recurse, then undo the choice. Every path from root to a full list is one unique permutation.
approach: Keep res, the current list cur and a boolean vis array.
dfs: if cur has n numbers, add a copy of cur to res and return.
Otherwise loop i over 0..n-1, skip if vis[i].
Mark vis[i], add nums[i], recurse, then remove the last element and unmark vis[i].
Return res.
dryRun: undo 3, undo 2, pick 3 -> [1,3], pick 2 -> [1,3,2], res gets [1,3,2]
undo back to [], pick 2 -> gives [2,1,3] and [2,3,1]

complexity.time: O(n * n!) since there are n! permutations and copying each costs n
complexity.space: O(n) for recursion, cur and vis (output not counted)

edgeCases: Single element gives one list
Max size n = 6 gives 720 lists
Negative numbers work, we never use values as indexes
Must add a new ArrayList copy, not cur itself, or all entries end up empty
problems.takeaway: Backtracking template: choose, recurse, un-choose. Use a vis array for 'each element once' problems.

problems.title: Sliding Window Maximum
problems.problem: A window of size k slides from left to right over the array, one step at a time. Return the maximum of each window.
problems.intuition: Keep a deque of indexes whose values are decreasing from front to back. If a new number is bigger than or equal to the back, the back can never be a window max again (the new number is bigger and lives longer), so pop it. The front is always the max of the current window; just drop it once it slides out.
approach: Use an int array q as a deque with head h and tail t.
For each i: if the front index q[h] <= i - k, it is outside the window, so h++.
While the back value nums[q[t-1]] <= nums[i], pop the back (t--).
Push i at the back.
Once i >= k - 1, ans[i - k + 1] = nums[q[h]].
Return ans.
dryRun: i=4: front 1 <= 4-3 so drop it; pop 3 and 2 (both <= 5); q = [4], ans[2] = 5

complexity.time: O(n) since each index is pushed and popped at most once
complexity.space: O(n) for the deque array (O(k) live entries)

edgeCases: k = 1: every element is its own max
k = n: one window, answer is the overall max
Strictly decreasing input: nothing is popped from the back, only from the front
Equal values: popping on <= keeps the newest index, which is fine
problems.takeaway: Max or min over a sliding window means a monotonic deque of indexes: pop smaller ones from the back, expired ones from the front.
